transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?
I can’t stop thinking about how old and wrong my face looks, and it’s getting in the way of me moving up at work. I really want to advance in my career, but this constant worry is holding me back.
Are these thoughts about your face intrusive and unwanted, or do they feel more like a genuine concern about your appearance that you can't stop focusing on?

To me, they feel like a very genuine concern because when I look in the mirror, I clearly see how aged and worn out my face looks, and I worry no one will take me seriously as a leader. At the same time, these thoughts are incredibly persistent and I simply cannot stop focusing on them, which has become completely overwhelming.
Do you recognize that your concern about your appearance might be exaggerated, or does it feel completely true and undeniable to you?

It feels completely true and undeniable to me, because when I look in the mirror, all I can see are these deep lines and sagging that make me look so worn out. I genuinely believe no one will take me seriously as a leader looking like this, and even though my husband and clients try to reassure me, it doesn't change what I see.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F45.2", "F42"], but based on this conversation, F42 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder) seems less likely because the patient does not experience the thoughts as intrusive or unwanted, but rather as a genuine and undeniable reflection of reality. This lack of insight is more consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.2). The patient's preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, despite reassurance, and the resulting functional impairment support maintaining F45.2 as the primary differential. No other disorders currently fit as well.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance—here, perceived facial aging—causing significant distress and functional impairment in occupational functioning. The belief is held with strong conviction, though not delusional intensity, and is resistant to reassurance, consistent with body dysmorphic disorder.
